results.comment: I think this stems from a problem of language and how it evolves.  People who argue over whether something is a work of art are really arguing over whether the work in question fits their own definition of art most of the time. I appreciate your attempt at clarification at 3:30 with encouraging people who "think they could do that" to instead state "this doesn't display a remarkable amount of technical skill, and that's what I really look for in art."  But you're basing that on your own definition: that art is something that can incorporate technical skill as an aspect, but is something bigger. Why is your definition of art more correct than theirs, though?  The word "art" comes from the same root as the word artisan: a skilled worker. A craftsperson. I don't enjoy sports, but I can appreciate pro athletes like football players who do flips into endzones, because that requires a lot of skill and honing of their craft.  It's artful.  Something lacking that technical skill might not be art to me.  If that's the case, it looks like we are using different definitions.  What you call art is what I would simply call creation, because those works certainly involved creativity. Understanding the creators can help us better appreciate their creations.  I think we can use words like creation and communication instead of trying to make the word "art" a synonym for them because I think the aspect of technical skill is most of its identity. All that being said, the point of words is as tools to communicate thought.  As long as you understand that your interpretation of words like "art" can be different that others, and are willing to take the best interpretation of another's statement, we'll all be fine.  For example, if someone says "I could do that" instead of schooling them on your view of what art is, you could simply reply "but it's pretty creative, no?"
